scenes.title: Input Variables — Types, Defaults, Validation
scenes.narration: Variables have appeared in five labs, always briefly. This lesson is their anatomy lesson: type, default, description — and validation blocks that reject impossible values before plan even runs.

scenes.narration: This is lab eighteen. Variables have been part of five labs now — lab eleven's map of objects, lab seventeen's sensitive password. Today we slow down on the declaration itself: what every variable can carry, and how to make the configuration reject bad input before it ever reaches a plan.

scenes.heading: Validation runs before plan
points: validation { condition, error_message } — attached to a variable
can(regex(...)): true if the expression succeeds — a shape gate
contains(list, value): the enum pattern
Failures happen locally in seconds — no wasted Azure calls
scenes.narration: Here's the idea that makes validation worth writing: it moves failure left. Without it, a bad value travels all the way to Azure and comes back as an error after a plan — or worse, creates something you didn't mean. With a validation block, the same bad value dies locally, in seconds, with a message you wrote. The two workhorse patterns: can plus regex for shape, contains for membership — the poor developer's enum.

scenes.narration: As always, the lab is in the course GitHub repository under Section 1, Foundations, with the link in the description. Readme, main dot t f, terraform dot t f — and the variables live in main dot t f this time, next to the logic that consumes them.

The simplest variable first, and it shows all three basic fields: type string, default eastus, description Azure region. A defaulted string is already useful — callers can override it, or ignore it entirely.

The second variable carries the first validation. Name prefix feeds the storage account's name, so it must obey Azure's lowercase alphanumeric naming — three to eighteen characters. The validation block says exactly that: can of regex, anchored at both ends, with an error message that tells the caller what to fix.

The third variable shows the other pattern. Tier should only ever be Standard or Premium — so the validation uses contains: is the value in this list? That's the enum pattern, built from two built-ins. Pass anything else, and Terraform refuses before planning.

And the consumption. The storage account's name comes from locals — prefix plus random suffix — and its tier comes straight from the validated variable. By the time this block runs, every value has already passed its gate.

scenes.caption: Validated inputs flow into the build
scenes.narration: Drawn out: three validated variables feed the configuration — the region into the resource group, the prefix into the assembled name, the tier into the storage account. Every arrow starts behind a gate that ran before plan.

steps.narration: Three variables enter the configuration — each one behind its own validation gate.
The region feeds the resource group; the prefix and tier feed the storage account.
The storage name is assembled in locals — prefix plus random suffix — then consumed.
Nothing reaches Azure unvalidated: every arrow starts behind a gate that ran before plan.

scenes.narration: Two runs tell the story. The apply succeeds with every default in place — three resources. But ask for a tier that isn't on the list, and the validation catches it before plan: invalid value for variable, tier must be Standard or Premium. Seconds, local, with a message you wrote. That's the gate doing its job.

scenes.heading: Common pitfall — trusting a default to catch typos
points: Defaults are silent: a misspelled region or tier passes straight through
validation runs before plan — it's your input gate, use it
error_message should say what to fix, not that something failed
Validation is for input rules — not for resource behavior
scenes.narration: Here are the pitfalls in this lab. One: defaults are silent — a misspelled region or tier passes straight through. A default supplies a value; it can't tell a typo from a choice. Two: validation runs before plan — it's your input gate, so use it. Without it, a bad value sails through plan and fails in Azure — or worse, deploys something you didn't intend. Three: the error message should say what to fix, not just that something failed. A good message names the rule, so bad input dies in seconds on your machine. Four: validation is for input rules — not for resource behavior. It checks what comes in, not what Terraform does with it afterward.

points: variable anatomy: type, default, description
validation blocks reject bad input before plan
can(regex(...)) gates the shape; contains(...) gates the choices
error_message is user-facing documentation — write it for the caller
Fail locally in seconds, not in Azure after a plan
scenes.narration: Quick recap — five things. One: variable anatomy — type, default, description. Two: validation blocks reject bad input before plan. Three: can with regex gates the shape; contains gates the choices. Four: the error message is user-facing documentation — write it for the caller. Five: fail locally in seconds — not in Azure after a plan.
Now that we understand how this Terraform configuration works, in the next part of this video, we'll move to a real-world demo and deploy it in Microsoft Azure.
